Partial-rapture writers allow that some believers are gathered before the lawless one is revealed and others later, according to their readiness.

Amillennial and postmillennial writers read the man of lawlessness either as a figure still to come just before the single return (Riddlebarger), or as a first-century figure linked to AD 70 (Gentry). In both, the gathering is the final return of Christ.
After the tribulation of those days
Is the gathering of the elect "after the tribulation" the rapture of the church, or a gathering of Israel or of saved people at the end?

Pretribulationists say the Olivet Discourse is addressed to the disciples as representatives of Israel. The "elect" are Jews and tribulation believers gathered for the kingdom (compare Isaiah 27:13). The church's rapture is not in view; it is a mystery Paul revealed later.
Midtribulationists also see this as the return to earth at the end of the week, separate from the earlier rapture at the middle.

Prewrath writers see this as the rapture. "The tribulation" here is the Antichrist's great tribulation (24:21), which is cut short (24:22). The cosmic signs then announce the day of the Lord (Joel 2:31), and the elect are gathered before the wrath falls.

This is the central text for posttribulationists. Jesus says the gathering comes "immediately after the tribulation". It has the same trumpet, clouds and angels as 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17. The elect are all believers, including the church.
Partial-rapture writers see this as the last gathering, which takes up believers who were not ready for the earlier rapture.

Preterist one-coming writers read verses 29-31 as the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70, told in the language of Old Testament prophecy, with "angels" as messengers of the gospel gathering the nations. Others in this group read them as the final return at the end of the age.
One taken, one left
Is the one "taken" raptured to safety, or taken away in judgment?
Many pretribulationists say this describes the return to earth, not the rapture. As in the flood (24:39), the ones taken are removed in judgment, and those left enter the kingdom.
Midtribulationists usually follow the pretribulational reading and apply it to the end of the week.
Prewrath writers read "taken" (paralambano, to take along) as taken to be with Christ, the same verb as in John 14:3. Those taken are rescued at the rapture just before the day of the Lord.

Posttribulationists also read "taken" as the gathering of the saints, at the single coming after the tribulation. They note that the passage follows directly from the gathering of the elect in verse 31.
Partial-rapture writers see here a selective removal of the watchful, followed by a warning to "watch" (24:42). Those left are believers who were not ready.

On this view the text describes the one coming as sudden and dividing. Some take the "taken" as gathered to Christ and others as swept away in judgment; either way it is the final return, not a hidden earlier event.
The seventh trumpet
Does the seventh trumpet mark the middle of the week, the end of the age, or the start of the final bowls?

Pretribulationists say the seventh trumpet is a judgment trumpet on the world, not a gathering trumpet for the church, so it is not Paul's last trumpet. It looks ahead to the bowls and the end of the week.
Midtribulationists see the seventh trumpet as Paul's last trumpet. They link it with the rise of the two witnesses (11:12) and the middle of the week, before the bowls of wrath in chapter 16.
Prewrath writers place the seventh trumpet late in the week, after the rapture at the sixth seal. It announces the final bowls and the reclaiming of the kingdom.

Posttribulationists say the seventh trumpet announces the end: the kingdom of the world becomes Christ's, and the time comes to judge the dead and reward the saints (11:18). That fits the end of the age and a single coming.
Amillennial writers read Revelation in parallel cycles. Each cycle (seals, trumpets, bowls) ends at the final judgment. The seventh trumpet, like the seventh seal and bowl, shows the end of history.
The sixth seal: the great day of their wrath has come
Does wrath begin at the sixth seal, or was it present from the first seal?

Pretribulationists say the Lamb opens all the seals, so all are his judgments. The people in 6:17 recognize that the wrath "has come", meaning it was already under way. So the whole week is wrath, and the church must be absent from it all.
Midtribulationists see the early seals as human and satanic evil. They place the start of God's wrath later, at the middle of the week.

This is the key text for prewrath. The sixth seal brings the darkened sun and moon that Joel 2:31 says come before the day of the Lord. Only then does the text say the day of wrath has come. The rapture (the great multitude, 7:9-14) comes between this signal and the trumpets.

Posttribulationists see the sixth seal as the cosmic signs at the very end, matching Matthew 24:29. They read the trumpets and bowls as overlapping with or repeating the seals, so the coming follows soon after.
Amillennial writers see the sixth seal as a picture of the final judgment at the one return. The seals cover the whole age from the cross to the end.
The seventieth week
Is Daniel's seventieth week still future and seven years long, or was it fulfilled in Christ?

Pretribulationists hold that the seventy weeks concern Daniel's people (9:24). A gap separates week 69 from week 70. The church age fills that gap, and the seventieth week resumes God's dealings with Israel, so the church is taken out first.
Midtribulationists agree the week is future. They stress that it divides at the middle, when the covenant is broken, and place the rapture at that point.
Prewrath writers agree the week is future. The abomination at the middle begins the great tribulation; the rapture comes later, when that persecution is cut short, during the second half.
Most posttribulationists accept a future seventieth week, but say Daniel gives no hint that the church is removed. The saints are present under the little horn (Daniel 7:21-22).
Partial-rapture writers accept the future week and see it as a time when unready believers are tested.

Many one-coming writers say the seventieth week was fulfilled in Christ: he confirmed the covenant and made sacrifice cease by his death (Hebrews 10:12-14), with AD 70 following. Others read the seventy weeks symbolically for the whole age. No gap of two thousand years is needed.
Imminence: the Lord could come at any moment

The New Testament tells believers to wait and watch for Christ himself, not for the Antichrist or the tribulation (Titus 2:13, James 5:8, 1 Thessalonians 1:10). Pretribulationists argue that if a seven-year tribulation had to come first, believers would look for signs, not for Christ. Only a rapture before the tribulation keeps the coming truly imminent.

Critics answer that "imminent" in the New Testament means near and certain, not "with no events before it". Jesus foretold events before his return, such as Peter's old age (John 21:18-19) and the gospel to all nations (Matthew 24:14). Paul said the day would not come until the apostasy (2 Thessalonians 2:3).

Pretribulationists reply that those events were either fulfilled early or did not stop the early church from expecting Christ at any time. 2 Thessalonians 2 speaks of the day of the Lord, not of the rapture. Expecting Christ, not the Antichrist, is the posture the epistles teach.
Israel, the church and the seventieth week

Daniel's seventy weeks are decreed for "your people and your holy city" (Daniel 9:24). Pretribulationists hold that God has distinct programs for Israel and the church. The church began at Pentecost after week 69, and the seventieth week returns to God's plan for Israel (Jeremiah 30:7, "the time of Jacob's trouble"). So the church is taken before the week begins.

Covenant and posttribulational writers reply that the New Testament makes Jew and Gentile one body (Ephesians 2:14-16) and calls the church the true circumcision (Philippians 3:3). Nothing in Daniel says the church must be absent. Also, believing Jews in the tribulation would themselves be part of the church.

Pretribulationists answer that unity in Christ does not erase God's national promises (Romans 11:25-29). The tribulation's focus on the twelve tribes (Revelation 7:4-8), the temple and Jerusalem fits a time when God is again dealing with Israel as a nation.
The restrainer is the Spirit in the church

In 2 Thessalonians 2:6-7 something (neuter) and someone (masculine) holds back the lawless one until "taken out of the way". Pretribulationists argue that only God can restrain Satan's man, and the Holy Spirit dwells in the church (1 Corinthians 3:16). When the church is removed, the Spirit's restraining work through it ends, and the lawless one appears.

Critics note that Paul never names the restrainer, and early writers such as Tertullian thought it was the Roman Empire. If the Spirit leaves, how are people saved during the tribulation? Gundry and others say the restrainer could be an angel (compare Daniel 10:13) or God's ordering of government.

Pretribulationists answer that the Spirit is not removed from the world, only his special restraining ministry through the indwelt church. He still works as he did before Pentecost. The neuter and masculine forms both fit the Spirit, since the Greek word for spirit is neuter.
Mortals are needed to enter the millennium

Isaiah 65:20 and Revelation 20:7-9 show people in the millennium who still die, sin and can rebel. Pretribulationists argue that if all believers are raptured and glorified at the end, and all unbelievers are judged (Matthew 25:31-46), no one in a mortal body is left to enter the kingdom. A pre-tribulation rapture allows people saved during the tribulation to enter it in mortal bodies.

Posttribulationists answer that mortal survivors can enter the kingdom without a gap: for example, Jews who believe as they see Christ (Zechariah 12:10, Romans 11:26) are converted at his coming and are not raptured. Amillennial writers say the problem only arises for those who expect a future earthly millennium.

Pretribulationists reply that anyone converted at the coming is a believer and should be raptured with the church under the posttrib model. A gap of time between the rapture and the return is the simplest way to explain who enters the kingdom alive.
The last trumpet is the seventh trumpet

Paul says the rapture happens at "the last trumpet" (1 Corinthians 15:52). Revelation numbers its trumpets, and the seventh is the last. Midtribulationists, such as Gleason Archer and Norman Harrison, note that at the seventh trumpet the mystery of God is finished (Revelation 10:7) and the saints are rewarded (11:18). They place it at the middle of the week.

Critics from both sides say Paul's readers could not have known Revelation's trumpets, so he cannot mean the seventh one. Others note that Revelation 11:15-18 points to the end of the age, not its middle, since it speaks of judging the dead.

Midtribulationists answer that the Spirit who inspired both books could join them. The seventh trumpet looks ahead to the end, but its sounding is placed before the bowls, which still lie ahead in chapters 15-16.
The two witnesses rise in the middle of the week

The two witnesses preach 1,260 days, are killed, and then hear "Come up here" and rise in a cloud (Revelation 11:3, 11:12). Midtribulationists see this as a picture of the church's rapture at the middle of the week, just before the seventh trumpet.

Critics say the witnesses are two individuals (or Israel's witness), not the whole church. Their rising after three and a half days need not fall at the middle of the week. Posttribulationists place their ministry in the second half.

Midtribulationists answer that the witnesses at least show a pattern: God's people bear witness, then are caught up in a cloud at a trumpet. The timing of 1,260 days fits half the week, and the trumpet follows at once.
Wrath belongs to the second half

Daniel 9:27, 7:25 and 12:7 divide the week at the middle. Jesus says great tribulation begins with the abomination (Matthew 24:15-21). Midtribulationists argue that the first half is a time of false peace and human evil, while the second half is God's wrath. The church, promised rescue from wrath (1 Thessalonians 5:9), is removed at the midpoint.

Pretribulationists say the seals in the first half are already the Lamb's judgments. Prewrath and posttrib writers say the great tribulation in the second half is persecution by the Antichrist, not God's wrath, so the midpoint is not the start of wrath.

Midtribulationists answer that the seals are general troubles like those Jesus called "the beginning of birth pains" (Matthew 24:8). The midpoint is the most clearly marked break in Daniel and Revelation, so it is the natural place for the church to leave.
Signs before, imminence after

Midtribulationists argue their view keeps both the New Testament signs and the hope. Believers will see the Antichrist's covenant and rise (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4), which explains why Paul and Jesus give signs to the church. Yet the rapture still comes before God's wrath, so the blessed hope (Titus 2:13) is rescue, not endurance of wrath.

Pretribulationists say any signs before the rapture destroy imminence. Posttribulationists say once the church is told to expect the Antichrist, there is no reason to stop at the middle; the signs Jesus gives (Matthew 24:29-30) come at the very end.

Midtribulationists answer that imminence means watching expectantly, not that nothing can come first. The middle of the week is the point where Scripture itself marks the turn from man's wrath to God's.
Tribulation is not wrath

Prewrath writers argue that the New Testament uses "tribulation" (thlipsis) for the suffering believers face from the world (John 16:33, Acts 14:22, Revelation 1:9), and "wrath" (orge) for God's judgment on the wicked. The great tribulation is the Antichrist's war on the saints (Revelation 13:7). The church is promised escape from wrath, not from tribulation.

Pretribulationists answer that the seals are opened by the Lamb and that the whole seventieth week is a single unit of God's judgment (Revelation 6:1). They argue that Jesus' "great tribulation" includes divine judgments, not only persecution.

Prewrath writers reply that the Lamb opening the seals does not mean every event in them is God's wrath; the fifth seal is the martyrs' cry for vengeance that has not yet come (Revelation 6:10). The text first says wrath "has come" only at the sixth seal (6:17).
Cosmic signs, then the day of the Lord

Joel 2:31 says the sun will be darkened and the moon turned to blood before the great day of the Lord. Matthew 24:29-31 puts the same signs after the great tribulation and before the gathering of the elect. Revelation 6:12-17 puts them at the sixth seal, just before wrath "has come". Prewrath writers argue that this sequence fixes the rapture after the tribulation is cut short but before the day of the Lord.

Pretribulationists say there may be more than one set of cosmic signs, and that the day of the Lord in Scripture can include the whole period. Posttribulationists say Matthew 24:29 puts the signs after the tribulation, not inside it, so the gathering is at the very end.

Prewrath writers answer that Jesus said the days would be "cut short" for the elect (Matthew 24:22). So the gathering ends the persecution early, before the end of the week. The order "signs, then wrath" is repeated in three separate texts.
The great multitude arrives in heaven

Revelation 7:9-14 shows a vast multitude from every nation standing before the throne, who "come out of the great tribulation". It appears after the sixth seal and before the seventh seal opens the trumpets. Prewrath writers see this as the raptured church, arriving suddenly between the signal of wrath and its outpouring.

Pretribulationists say the multitude are those saved and martyred during the tribulation, not the church. Posttribulationists say the scene is a vision of the end that need not fit a timeline. Amillennial writers read it as the whole redeemed people seen at the last day.
Prewrath writers answer that the group is too large and too sudden to be only martyrs. It appears at the exact place where the sequence of Matthew 24 puts the gathering of the elect.
Believers will see the Antichrist first

Paul tells believers that the day of the Lord and "our gathering to him" will not come until the apostasy and the revealing of the man of lawlessness (2 Thessalonians 2:1-4). Jesus warns his followers to flee when they see the abomination (Matthew 24:15-16). Kurschner argues that these warnings are only useful if the church is present to see them.

Pretribulationists answer that 2 Thessalonians 2 concerns the day of the Lord, not the rapture, and that Matthew 24 addresses Jewish believers in Judea. They note that Paul comforts the church rather than preparing it to face the Antichrist.

Prewrath writers reply that Paul links "the coming" and "our gathering" in one phrase (2:1) and then gives events that come before it. Jesus' warnings are given to the same disciples who received the Great Commission, the founders of the church.
"Immediately after the tribulation"

Jesus places his coming and the gathering of the elect "immediately after the tribulation of those days" (Matthew 24:29-31). Posttribulationists argue that this is the plainest timing statement in Scripture. The same features appear in 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17: descent, trumpet, clouds and gathering. Ladd and Gundry see no reason to split them.

Pretribulationists say Matthew 24 is about Israel and the elect are tribulation saints. Prewrath writers agree it is the rapture but say "those days" are cut short, so it falls before the end of the week.

Posttribulationists reply that the disciples who heard the discourse became the church, and the parallels with Paul are too close to be two events. Cutting the days short means God limits the tribulation, not that a gap opens before the end.
Apantesis: meeting to escort the king

Paul uses apantesis for meeting the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4:17). Peterson and others argue it was a term for a city's delegation going out to greet a visiting dignitary and then escorting him back. Luke uses it this way when believers come out to meet Paul and walk with him to Rome (Acts 28:15). So the church rises to meet Christ and returns with him to earth.

Cosby argues the word was not a fixed technical term. Pretribulationists add that in Matthew 25:6 the virgins meet the bridegroom and go in with him to the feast, not back out. The direction after the meeting must come from context.

Posttribulationists agree it is not strictly technical, but say the usual pattern is escort, and both Acts 28:15 and Matthew 25:6 show the welcoming party joining the arriving figure at his destination. Christ's destination in 1 Thessalonians 4 is earth.
The New Testament knows one second coming

The New Testament uses the same words (parousia, apokalypsis, epiphaneia) for the coming that believers hope for and the coming that destroys the lawless one (1 Thessalonians 4:15, 2 Thessalonians 2:8). Hebrews 9:28 speaks of Christ appearing "a second time". Posttribulationists argue that no text clearly describes a coming in two stages seven years apart.

Pretribulationists answer that the same words also describe the first coming, so shared words do not prove a single event. They point to contrasts: a coming for the saints in the air versus with the saints to earth (Zechariah 14:5, Jude 14), a coming with no signs versus one after signs.

Posttribulationists reply that the "contrasts" are different aspects of one event, as the meeting in the air leads into the return. The burden is on those who see two comings to show a text that teaches it, not one that permits it.
Saints are present in the tribulation

Revelation repeatedly shows "saints" on earth during the tribulation: the beast makes war on them (13:7), they need endurance (14:12), and they keep the testimony of Jesus (12:17). Daniel 7:21-22 also shows the saints under the little horn until the Ancient of Days comes. Posttribulationists argue that these are the church, which has always grown under persecution.

Pretribulationists say these saints are people converted after the rapture, perhaps through the 144,000 or the two witnesses. The fact that the word "church" does not appear in chapters 4-19 is significant, they argue.

Posttribulationists answer that "saints" is Paul's normal word for the church (for example 1 Corinthians 1:2). A large new body of believers, saved after the church and the Spirit's restraining work are gone, is harder to explain than the church's presence.
A reward for the watchful

Jesus tells his disciples to watch and pray "that you may be counted worthy to escape all these things" (Luke 21:36). Hebrews 9:28 says he will appear to those who eagerly wait for him. Partial-rapture writers such as Robert Govett and G. H. Lang argue that the first rapture is a reward for faithful, watchful believers, while others remain to be purified in the tribulation.

Critics in every camp answer that this makes rapture depend on works. It divides the body of Christ, which Paul says will be changed "all" together (1 Corinthians 15:51). In 1 Thessalonians 5:10 Paul says believers will live with Christ "whether we wake or sleep".

Partial-rapture writers reply that salvation is by grace, but rewards and the timing of entry into the kingdom depend on faithfulness, as in the parable of the virgins (Matthew 25:1-13). The "all" of 1 Corinthians 15:51 refers to all who are raptured at that time.
Answering the charge of salvation by works

Critics say partial rapture teaches salvation by works. Partial-rapture writers answer that it does not touch salvation. All believers are saved and will share in the final resurrection. The question is reward: Paul himself strove to "attain" a special resurrection (Philippians 3:11-14), and believers can suffer loss while still being saved (1 Corinthians 3:15).

Other views reply that Philippians 3:11 speaks of the resurrection all believers share, and 1 Corinthians 3:15 speaks of judging works, not of being left behind. The rapture is part of salvation itself, given to those "in Christ" (1 Thessalonians 4:16), not to the most faithful.

Partial-rapture writers answer that "in Christ" names the whole group raised at some point, but Scripture also speaks of firstfruits (Revelation 14:4) and of being "counted worthy" (Luke 21:36). God can distinguish timing without distinguishing salvation.
One visible return ends the age

Amillennial and postmillennial writers note that the New Testament links Christ's one return with the resurrection of all the dead (John 5:28-29), the judgment of all nations (Matthew 25:31-32), and the renewal of creation (2 Peter 3:10-13). They argue there is no room for a secret rapture, a seven-year gap, or a later return. The church is gathered when every eye sees him (Revelation 1:7).

Premillennialists answer that Revelation 20 places a thousand years between two resurrections. Pretribulationists add that texts which compress events, like Old Testament prophecy, can still describe events separated by time.

One-coming writers reply that Revelation 20 is a symbolic vision best read through the clearer teaching passages. Jesus says the resurrection of the just and the unjust happens in "an hour" (John 5:28-29), and believers are raised on "the last day" (John 6:40).
The great tribulation was AD 70

Preterist one-coming writers such as Gentry and Mathison note that Jesus told those in Judea to flee (Matthew 24:16) and said "this generation" would not pass away until these things happened (24:34). Luke says Jerusalem would be surrounded by armies (Luke 21:20). They read the great tribulation as the Roman war and the fall of the temple in AD 70, already past.

Futurists answer that Jesus calls it the worst tribulation ever, never to be equalled (Matthew 24:21), and connects it directly to his visible return (24:29-30), which has not happened. They take "this generation" to mean the generation that sees these signs.

Preterists reply that "never to be equalled" is a common prophetic formula (compare Ezekiel 5:9 on the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC). The "coming on the clouds" uses Old Testament judgment language (Isaiah 19:1). The final, bodily return is taught in other passages (Acts 1:11) and is still future.
Tribulation marks the whole age

Many amillennialists read "tribulation" as the normal experience of the church between Christ's comings (John 16:33, Acts 14:22). John calls himself a partner "in the tribulation" (Revelation 1:9). Hendriksen and Riddlebarger argue that the troubles of Revelation repeat across the whole age, with a short, intense time of evil just before the end, followed by the one return.

Futurists say this reading flattens specific details, like 1,260 days and 42 months, which point to a defined period. Dispensationalists add that Daniel's seventieth week must be seven literal years if the first sixty-nine weeks were literal.

Amillennialists answer that Revelation is full of symbolic numbers and that the 1,260 days in Revelation 12 cover the time from Christ's ascension (12:5-6). The seventy weeks are a symbolic period that reach their goal in Christ (Daniel 9:24-27).
The witness of the historic church

One-coming writers note that the early fathers expected the church to face the Antichrist (Didache 16, Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.25-30). The creeds confess one return of Christ to judge the living and the dead. They argue that a pretribulation rapture as a system emerged only in the 1830s, with John Nelson Darby.

Pretribulationists answer that truth is settled by Scripture, not by dates. They also point to possible earlier hints, such as Pseudo-Ephraem (possibly 4th-7th century) and Morgan Edwards (1788), though the meaning of these texts is disputed.

One-coming writers reply that Pseudo-Ephraem most likely speaks of believers being gathered to the Lord in a spiritual sense, not removed before a tribulation; this too is disputed. Even if hints exist, the historic church did not teach two comings.
Irenaeus and Hippolytus

Irenaeus of Lyons (about 180) and Hippolytus of Rome (about 204) expected the church to suffer under the Antichrist before Christ returns and raises the righteous. Posttribulationists cite them as the early pattern. Pretribulationists answer that the fathers did not address the question in modern terms.
Pseudo-Ephraem sermon (disputed)

A Latin sermon falsely attributed to Ephraem the Syrian, dated between about 373 and 627, says the saints are 'taken to the Lord' before the coming trouble. Some read this as an early pre-tribulation rapture. Others argue it means death or protection and that the text expects believers to face the Antichrist. Its meaning is disputed.
Morgan Edwards

Baptist pastor Morgan Edwards, in an essay written as a student in 1742-44 and published in 1788, placed the rapture of the saints about three and a half years before the end. Pretribulationists cite him as a forerunner. Others note his gap is shorter than seven years and could be called mid-tribulational.

The Chilean Jesuit Manuel Lacunza wrote in the 1790s, under the name Juan Josafat Ben-Ezra, and his book was printed in 1812. He taught a future return and placed a short interval between Christ's coming in the air and his arrival on earth. Its link to the later pre-tribulation view is debated.
Edward Irving and the Albury conferences

From 1826 to 1830 Henry Drummond hosted prophecy conferences at Albury Park in England. Edward Irving translated Lacunza into English in 1827. These meetings revived premillennial hope in Britain and helped shape the setting in which later rapture teaching grew.
Margaret MacDonald (disputed influence)

In 1830 Margaret MacDonald of Port Glasgow, Scotland, described a vision of Christ's coming. Dave MacPherson and others argue it was the source of Darby's pre-tribulation view. Pretribulationists and many historians answer that her vision expects believers to be tested by the Antichrist and that Darby reached his view by his own Bible study. The link is disputed.

John Nelson Darby, an Anglican clergyman who joined the Brethren, taught a secret, any-moment rapture distinct from Christ's visible return. He developed the view between about 1827 and 1833, and presented it at the Powerscourt conferences in Ireland (1831-33). It rested on a sharp distinction between Israel and the church.
Plymouth Brethren divide

The Brethren spread Darby's teaching through Britain and abroad. Benjamin Wills Newton, a Brethren leader at Plymouth, rejected the secret rapture and held that the church would pass through the tribulation. The 1845-48 dispute between Newton and Darby helped split the movement.
Robert Govett and the partial rapture

Robert Govett, an English preacher at Norwich, taught from the 1850s that only watchful believers would be raptured before the tribulation. G. H. Pember, D. M. Panton and later Watchman Nee carried this partial-rapture view forward.
Niagara Bible Conference divides

The Niagara Bible Conference (1878-1897) spread premillennial teaching in North America. In the 1890s its leaders split over the rapture. Robert Cameron, Nathaniel West and W. J. Erdman became posttribulational, while James Brookes, A. C. Gaebelein and C. I. Scofield stayed pretribulational. The conference ended in 1897, and a successor gathering in 1901 also failed to unite them.

C. I. Scofield's study Bible (1909, revised 1917) placed pre-tribulational and dispensational notes beside the biblical text. It became the most influential channel of the view among English-speaking evangelicals for most of the twentieth century.

Lewis Sperry Chafer founded the Evangelical Theological College in 1924, renamed Dallas Theological Seminary in 1936. Through Chafer, John Walvoord, J. Dwight Pentecost and Charles Ryrie it became the leading academic centre of pretribulational teaching.
